abstract.t: The document introduces an optional, new type of SNPs called Hierarchical SNP (HSNP) that can compress the traditional CSNPs during stable network conditions into a variant of merkle tree, hence allowing to support very large databases and adjacency numbers due to vastly reduced size of CSNP exchanges. Such an approach leads also in case of inconsistencies to much faster re-synchronization since only a subset of CSNPs is necessary to correct the entropy present.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The document introduces an optional, new type of SNPs called Hierarchical SNP (HSNP) that can compress the traditional CSNPs during stable network conditions into a variant of merkle tree, hence allowing to support very large databases and adjacency numbers due to vastly reduced size of CSNP exchanges. Such an approach leads also in case of inconsistencies to much faster re-synchronization since only a subset of CSNPs is necessary to correct the entropy present.

Although the scheme can be applied recursively to the point where a single merkle hash represents the whole database, for practical purposes a two level tree allows compression for LSDB sizes of the 1E5 order and hence the document limits itself in examples to such magnitudes. Further considerations mentioned in
seem to make this limit practically prudent.
We call CSNP entries of LSPs the first level merkle hash (where we basically use lsp id, seq# and checksum as "hash") and the hash summarizing a set of those second level merkle hash and so on.

section.title: Dynamic Leaf Partitioning
section.t: Practically speaking, the most interesting problem is the correct subdivision of the database into first level collection of leaf nodes (CSNP entries) that on one hand do provide a good compression, on the other hand the subdivision cannot change too often, otherwise the neighbor receiving the information may have to recompute the hashes rather than relying on a cache representing its own merkle tree.

A first example will serve well here. We limit ourselves in the examples to consideration of a LSDB with 64 nodes with system identifiers of 1000.0000.00<node-id> and 128 fragments 0 to 32. We leave the uneven node identifiers out to have some "holes" in the numbering to hit some corner cases in examples. We disregard the pseudo node byte as simply another byte of system identifier since it does not contribute further details to the scheme.

Each of such fragments when advertised as CSNP entry consumes LSP ID + Fragment + Seq# + CSUM + Lifetime length which amounts to 8 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 14 bytes. We can fit into the prevailing 1500 bytes somewhat less than 100 of such entries. Since it is desirable to produce one packet on a miss on the merkle hash of first level leaf the examples will focus, which tactically is also an implementation guidance, on leaves containing around 80 fragments with some exceptions. Why we do not try to maximize the "packing" since LSDB may grow and to maximize the chances of "leaf packing" on both sides of an adjacency and hence use of hashes some "slack" is advisable.

The packing will always put all fragments of a system into same leaf (which of course can exceed the advisable 80 fragments sometimes) and a leaf will be split into two 2nd order leaves once the 80 fragments are exceeded otherwise. Once two 2nd order leaves can be merged into one leaf with less than 80 fragments they will be. The CSNP entries (or equivalently, we can just talk about fragments) are sorted on their usual <system-id.fragment> numbering.

middle.section:
Since we need to generate massive amount of hashes over sets of ever changing fragments it is very desirable to use a specialized hash function that provides means for very fast incremental adjustment of hash result on fragments arriving, aging out or changing their checksums. Also, splitting or merging of leaves should allow to generate 2nd order and above hashes very quickly.
Deeper considerations on such hashes can be found in
but the design space is simplified due to irrelevance of security involved.
The hash function is a very fast XOR operation which incorporates the numbering of fragments. It is 64 bits long for simplicity. Symbol << is used for rotation to the left.
A hash of a first order leave is nothing but (where all used values are converted to 64 bit values first with any remaining high order bits zero'ed out) XOR(hash, (system-id-of-fragment + 1) << fragment#) followed by XOR(hash, (fragment# + 1) << 32 | (fragment-seq# + 1) << 16 | (fragment-csum + 1)) for all contained fragments . Obviously, such an operation can be easily reversed to yield the previous hash without the fragment which allows for very fast removal, addition of fragments and updates of the relevant fields.
A hash of second order leave is nothing but XOR of all the hashes of its contained first order leaves with. Again, this allows to update the hash be adding, removing a leaf or changing its hash in a very fast and simple manner. The same packing logic of keeping 80 first order leaves in a second order leaves applies. This will cause a mismatch in the hash of a 2nd order leaf to advertise roughly a PDU full of first order leaves.
Ultimately, and fairly obviously, third order hash uses second order hash logic to keep its hash. However, the question remains. This all means that every time a first order leaf changes the contained system IDs for some reason the merkle hashes will have to be readjusted recursively in according 2nd and third order leaves. This is in itself nothing particular since any change on first order leaf hash forces change on second order and consequently third order leaf hash. This is how Merkle trees work after all.

section.title: Acknowledgement
section.t: The discussions about "compressing CSNPs" go very long way back, to the times Radia Perlman were allegedly stalking the halls with insomniac Dave Katz. Recent efforts to push the scale of the protocol to new heights made the effort worth the effort (pun intended) to codify it into a working engineering solution.
